tip: 못 (mot) = couldn't, 안 (an) = chose not to: 못 샀어요 (mot sasseoyo = couldn't buy it). With 안 it would mean you decided against it.
Past 'it was X': 이었어요 after consonants — 만 원이었어요 (man wonieosseoyo = it was 10,000 won).
'There was' needs only one verb: 회의가 있었어요 (hoeuiga isseosseoyo = there was a meeting) – 있다 (itda) also covers 'had', as in 'I had a meeting'.
시작하다 (sijakada) works both ways: 회의가 시작했어요 = it started; 회의를 시작했어요 = (I) started it.

english: I had a lot of work today.
tip: 일이 많았어요 (iri manasseoyo), literally 'work was many' — Korean for 'I was swamped.'
잘 됐어요 (jal dwaesseoyo) = 'it went well' — also the response to good news: 'great!'

english: I didn't go to work today.
tip: 안 (an = not) sits right before the verb: 회사에 안 갔어요 (hoesae an gasseoyo = didn't go to work) – never at the front like English 'didn't'.

english: I stayed in Seoul for a week.
tip: Duration needs no particle: 일주일 있었어요 (iljuil isseosseoyo = stayed a week).
로 (ro) marks the means: 비행기로 갔어요 (bihaenggiro gasseoyo = went by plane). After most consonants it becomes 으로 (euro).
길을 잃었어요 (gireul ireosseoyo) = 'I got lost' — literally 'lost the road.'
No 's needed: 할머니 집 (halmeoni jip = Grandma's house) – Korean stacks the nouns and the possessive 의 (ui) usually drops out.
Honor elders with -(으)시-: 할머니가 만드셨어요 (mandeusyeosseoyo = made, honorific).

english: My younger sibling came home yesterday.
tip: 동생 (dongsaeng) is any younger sibling – no gender. Add 여 (yeo) or 남 (nam) only when it matters: 여동생 (yeodongsaeng) = younger sister.
전화하다 (jeonhwahada = to call) takes 한테 (hante), not 을/를 (eul/reul): 엄마한테 전화했어요 (eommahante jeonhwahaesseoyo = called my mom).
Parents get -(으)시- too: 사셨어요 (sasyeosseoyo = bought, honorific).
결혼했어요 (gyeolhonhaesseoyo) covers both 'got married' and 'is married.'

english: A friend gave me a present.
tip: No 'to me' needed: 선물을 줬어요 (seonmureul jwosseoyo = gave me a present) – with 주다 (juda = give), an unmentioned receiver is understood as the speaker.

english: I hung out with a friend on the weekend.
tip: 놀다 (nolda) isn't just for kids — adults use 놀았어요 for 'hung out.'
Rain 'comes' in Korean: 비가 왔어요 (biga wasseoyo = it rained).
눈 (nun) = snow and also 'eye' — 눈이 왔어요 can only mean it snowed.
몸이 아팠어요 (momi apasseoyo) = 'I was sick' — literally 'my body hurt.'
병원에 갔어요 (byeongwone gasseoyo) usually means seeing a doctor – Koreans say 병원 (byeongwon = hospital) for any clinic visit, however minor.
Korean 'eats' medicine: 약을 먹어요 (yageul meogeoyo = take medicine).

english: I went to bed early yesterday.
tip: 자다 (jada) covers both 'sleep' and 'go to bed': 일찍 잤어요 (iljjik jasseoyo) = went to bed early, not only 'slept early'.
잘 잤어요? (jal jasseoyo) = 'did you sleep well?' — a warm morning greeting at home.
시간 (sigan) counts hours of duration, 시 (si) tells clock time: 열 시간 잤어요 (yeol sigan jasseoyo = slept ten hours) – 열 시 (yeol si) is 10 o'clock.

english: I read two books over the weekend.
tip: 권 (gwon) counts books: 두 권 (du gwon = two volumes) — native numbers before counters.
다 (da = all) goes before the verb, not the noun: 숙제를 다 했어요 (sukjereul da haesseoyo) – literally 'homework, all did'.

english: What are you going to do tomorrow?
tip: (으)ㄹ 거예요 (l geoyeyo) = 'going to' — Korean's everyday future: 할 거예요 = will do.

english: I'm going to meet a friend tomorrow.
tip: 내일 (naeil = tomorrow) never takes 에 (e) – it stands bare. Weekdays do: 토요일에 (toyoire = on Saturday). Yesterday, today and tomorrow all drop the particle.
